html:
The Statute of Kalisz was a charter of rights for Jews issued on 8 September 1264 by Bolesław the Pious, Duke of Greater Poland, in the town of Kalisz. It gave Jews protection and a legal standing that helped make Poland the home of Europe's largest Jewish community.

It placed the Jews under the duke's direct protection. Among its terms:

  • matters among Jews were judged in Jewish courts, and cases between Jews and Christians by special judges
  • harming a Jew or desecrating a Jewish cemetery or synagogue was punished heavily
  • Christians were forbidden to accuse Jews of using Christian blood, a charge then spreading in Europe
  • Jews were free to trade, travel and lend money

Many rulers in Europe were expelling or persecuting Jews in these centuries. Polish kings extended the statute to the whole kingdom, Casimir the Great in 1334 and others after him. Jews moving east from the German lands found refuge, and by the 16th century Poland-Lithuania was the centre of Jewish life in Europe, a world that lasted until the Holocaust.
